paragraphs.heading: What it is
paragraphs.text: Translation is how cells make proteins, using RNA molecules as templates. The protein is a chain of amino acids, and their order is set by the order of nucleotides in the RNA. The work is done by ribosomes, large complexes of RNA and proteins. The finished chain, called a polypeptide, folds into a working protein, and it can even begin folding while it is still being made.

paragraphs.heading: Reading in threes
paragraphs.text: The RNA is read three nucleotides at a time. Each group of three, called a codon, adds one particular amino acid to the growing chain. The matching of codons to amino acids is the genetic code. Because each new amino acid matches the next codon along the messenger RNA (mRNA), the order of the codons decides the order of the amino acids.

paragraphs.heading: The protein factory
paragraphs.text: Messenger RNA carries genetic information from the chromosomes to the ribosomes, which work outside the nucleus. A ribosome is the cell's factory for assembling amino acids into proteins. In eukaryotes it has two parts, a small 40S subunit and a large 60S subunit. These come together before translation begins, giving the work a place to happen.

paragraphs.heading: Transfer RNA, the carrier
paragraphs.text: Amino acids are brought to the ribosome by transfer RNA (tRNA), small RNA chains of 74 to 93 nucleotides. Each tRNA has a spot to hold an amino acid and an anticodon, a three-nucleotide sequence that pairs with the matching codon on the mRNA. Enzymes called aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases attach the right amino acid to each tRNA, which is then said to be charged. If they attach the wrong one, the protein can end up with an incorrect amino acid. This mistranslation happens at low levels in most organisms.

paragraphs.heading: Inside the ribosome
paragraphs.text: Translation has three stages: initiation, elongation and termination. The ribosome has two binding sites for tRNA. The A site takes in an incoming tRNA whose anticodon matches the codon, and the P/E site holds the tRNA attached to the growing chain. The ribosome moves along the mRNA toward its 3' end. Each new amino acid joins at the end of the chain called the C-terminus, which is why translation is described as running from amine to carboxyl.
